project.objective: When and where did Anders Monsen marry Unna Halsteinsdatter, and what does the marriage record show?

questions.question: When and where did Anders Monsen marry Unna Halsteinsdatter?
questions.rationale: The marriage date and place of Anders Monsen and Unna Halsteinsdatter are the central unknowns of this research objective. Norwegian patronymic naming conventions (Monsen = son of Mons; Halsteinsdatter = daughter of Halstein) place this research in a Norwegian context where digitized church records (kirkebøker) are available through Digitalarkivet and FamilySearch. Norwegian parish registers typically recorded marriage date, place, names of parties, their parents, and witnesses — all of which bear directly on the research objective. This is a single-event question (one marriage) that can be resolved by locating and extracting the marriage entry.

exhaustive_declaration.justification: overturn_risk and repository_breadth block. The two MCP-addressable gaps named in the prior declaration (Norway Census 1870, collection 4135961; Norway Probate Index Cards 1640-1903, collection 1661306) have now been searched and returned negative results (pli_007/log_061-062; pli_008/log_063-065). One gap remains that prevents declaration: Digitalarkivet.no — the Norwegian National Archives website holding the Hordaland parish church book images (Kinsarvik, Ulvik, Granvin, Voss) — is freely and publicly accessible but requires human browser navigation; MCP tools cannot reach it. This is not an inaccessible or sealed source: it is the primary repository for these records and is fully accessible to a human researcher at no cost. FamilySearch volume_search (log_032) confirmed FamilySearch holds zero digitized church book image volumes for the Hordaland parishes where Halsteinsdatter names concentrate (per log_016 and loc_001). FamilySearch's two national marriage/church-book indices (collections 1468080 and 4237104) returned zero results across all name variants. Norway civil registration did not begin until 1876 (loc_001; wiki_read performed); for the period of this marriage the Lutheran parish register is the sole vital system. The marriage register for Unna Halsteinsdatter's home parish is the single most decisive record type — it sits at Digitalarkivet.no, which has not been searched. A freely accessible source of this directness and relevance constitutes an unsearched gap, not a pursued-and-unavailable source. The narrow inaccessibility exception does not apply. Research must be completed by a human researcher at Digitalarkivet.no before exhaustiveness can be declared.

stop_criteria.goal_alignment: Fails. No marriage record for Anders Monsen and Unna Halsteinsdatter was found in any searched repository. Every FamilySearch-indexed Norwegian marriage and church-book collection (collections 1468080 and 4237104) returned zero results across all name variants (Unna/Una/Unne; Halsteinsdatter/fatherGivenName Halstein; Anders Monsen/fatherGivenName Mons). Norwegian census records (1865, 1870, 1875, 1891, 1900) and probate index cards (1640-1903) were searched and returned no match. The question (date, place, and content of the marriage record) remains entirely unanswered. Failure is attributable to the decisive source being in an unsearched repository (Digitalarkivet.no), not to confirmed destruction or unavailability of records.
stop_criteria.repository_breadth: BLOCKING FAILURE. FamilySearch's national marriage index (1468080) and church books index (4237104) were exhausted with all name variants. Norway censuses 1865 (3756102), 1870 (4135961), 1875 (1529106), 1891 (4067726), and 1900 (3744863) were searched — all negative. Norway Probate Index Cards 1640-1903 (1661306) searched — negative (log_063-065; above-threshold hits were Mons Monsen in Bergen 1782-1796, chronologically incompatible). FamilySearch volume_search (log_032) confirmed no digitized church book image volumes exist for the Hordaland parishes (Kinsarvik, Ulvik, Vikoor, Voss). Digitalarkivet.no — the primary free repository for Norwegian church records, holding browse-only parish register images for these exact parishes — has not been searched. It is accessible to a human researcher at no cost. This is an unsearched repository, not an inaccessible one. Ancestry.com (pli_005) was also skipped as requiring a paid subscription and human navigation. FAN research through collateral relatives (siblings of Anders or Unna) was not attempted and could help narrow the parish for targeted Digitalarkivet browsing.
stop_criteria.original_substitution: Not yet assessable. Indexed FamilySearch records (derivatives) were the search vehicle throughout. The original parish registers are held on Digitalarkivet.no, which has not been searched. No original register images have been accessed or examined. This criterion cannot be evaluated until the source repository holding the originals has been consulted.
stop_criteria.independent_verification: Not assessable — no marriage record has been located in any searched repository. There is nothing to independently verify. Criterion fails by default in the absence of any positive finding.
stop_criteria.evidence_class: Fails. No original record with primary information about this marriage has been found. Zero marriage records were identified for this couple across all searched repositories. The original parish registers on Digitalarkivet.no have not been consulted.
stop_criteria.conflict_resolution: Passes vacuously. No evidence was found and no conflicts are registered. Nothing to resolve.
stop_criteria.overturn_risk: High — fails. Digitalarkivet.no holds browse-only parish register images for Kinsarvik, Ulvik, Granvin, and Voss (the Hordaland parishes where Halsteinsdatter names concentrate per log_016 and loc_001). FamilySearch confirmed it holds no digitized image volumes for these parishes (log_032). Norway civil registration did not begin until 1876 (loc_001; wiki_read performed in prior invocation); for the period of this marriage the Lutheran parish register is the sole vital system. The marriage register for Unna Halsteinsdatter's home parish is the single most decisive record type and sits in an unsearched, freely accessible repository. An unsearched source of this directness — one that would directly answer the question if the marriage is recorded — constitutes high overturn risk. The narrow inaccessibility exception does not apply because Digitalarkivet.no is publicly accessible at no cost; its inaccessibility is only to MCP tools, not to human researchers.

items.rationale: FamilySearch collection 1468080 'Norway, Marriages, 1660-1926' — 1,330,979 indexed records, nationwide coverage, free. Search for 'Anders Monsen' and 'Unna Halsteinsdatter' and variants (Halsteinsd., Hallsteinsdatter, Halstend., Una). Per loc_001: this is a legacy partial-coverage collection — a hit requires verification against the original image; a negative result does not rule out the marriage. Norwegian marriages were recorded in the bride's home parish. First and highest-probability sweep because it is a dedicated national marriage index.

FamilySearch collection 4237104 'Norway, Church Books, 1797-1958' — 14,398,439 records, index AND images, the best FamilySearch option per loc_001. Covers baptisms, confirmations, marriages, and burials. If a marriage record is found, retrieve the image: post-1830s entries include fathers' names and birthplaces of both parties (directly serving the 'what does the record show?' component). Search name variants for Halsteinsdatter: the -datter suffix was frequently abbreviated as d., dr., dtr. in records.

Digitalarkivet.no (Norwegian National Archives) browse-based search cannot be executed autonomously — external site requires human browsing. URL generated and logged (log_022). This is the highest-priority remaining source for Norwegian church records. Skipped for autonomous session per BCG Standard 18 (inaccessible resource); must be completed by a human researcher using the generated URL: https://www.digitalarkivet.no/en/search/persons/advanced?firstname=Unna&lastname=Halsteinsdatter, focusing on Ulvik, Kinsarvik, Granvin, and Voss parishes in Hordaland.

If the marriage is not found through national indices (steps 1-3), census records establish where Anders Monsen and Unna Halsteinsdatter lived, identifying the specific parish whose registers must be searched. Per loc_001: parish identification is prerequisite to effective parish-level searching in patronymic-era Norway. FamilySearch holds indexed+images for 1865 (collection 3756102), 1870 (4135961), 1891 (4067726), and 1900 (3744863). Search for Anders Monsen and Unna (wife), and also for Mons Monsen (likely Anders's father per his patronymic Monsen) to locate the family's farm and parish. A census locating the family provides the parish name needed to browse specific church-book volumes.

items.repository: Digitalarkivet.no (Norwegian National Archives, free public website)
items.rationale: All FamilySearch-indexed and full-text-searchable collections have been exhausted. The Lutheran parish marriage registers for Hordaland parishes where Halsteinsdatter names concentrate (Ulvik, Kinsarvik, Granvin, Voss) are held at Digitalarkivet.no as scanned images. Norwegian civil registration began in 1876, so the parish register is the sole vital system for a marriage in the 1840s-1860s. Digitalarkivet.no is free and publicly accessible but requires human browser navigation. Search for Unna Halsteinsdatter (also Una, Unne; Halstensdr., Halsteinsd.) and Anders Monsen across Hordaland marriage registers.

Collection 4067726 (Norway Census 1891) was previously searched for Unna Halsteinsdatter (log_020, zero results) but was NOT searched for Anders Monsen with a Hordaland residencePlace filter. Anders was born approximately 1837–1840 and would be approximately 51–54 years old in 1891. The 1891 census is fully indexed and name-searchable. Finding Anders with wife Unna in this census would establish their residence parish, which is the key piece of information needed to target Digitalarkivet.no parish register searches. The groom search in collection 1468080 (log_039) produced only a wrong candidate (Anders Monsen Røsland, b. 1853, father Mons Endresen — not Mons Monsen), so census household placement is the next feasible avenue for locating the marriage parish.

Collection 3744863 (Norway Census 1900) was previously searched for Unna Halsteinsdatter (log_021, two wrong results) but was NOT searched for Anders Monsen with a Hordaland residencePlace filter. Anders would be approximately 60–63 in 1900. The 1900 Norwegian census is particularly detailed — it records birth county (amt), church parish (prestegjeld), and children's birth years, which could establish the residence parish and help bracket the marriage year range via children's ages. If pli_010 (1891 census) fails to locate Anders, this 1900 search using the same subject identifier is the next best census source. Anders's birth ~1837–1840 limits the date window to the creator's lifespan; the 1900 census closing date falls within that range.

Collection 1529106 (Norway Census 1875) covers all of Norway and is fully name-indexed. It was not searched for Anders Monsen with a Hordaland residencePlace filter. The 1875 census is strategically the most valuable untried census source: if Anders (~35-38 years old in 1875) and Unna married in the 1860s, the 1875 household would likely include young children born post-marriage, revealing both the residence parish and bracketing the marriage year. The 1891 (pli_010) and 1900 (pli_011) searches were both negative, suggesting Anders may have died before 1891 or appears under a farm name; the 1875 census predates that window and may still find him. The 1870 Bergen-city census (pli_007, collection 4135961) covered only Bergen city and cannot speak to inner Hardanger parishes.

Norway Marriages 1660-1926 at FamilySearch (collection 1468080) is a legacy collection — index only, not complete for any parish; verify any hit with the original image in Digitalarkivet or the Church Books collection (4237104).
Digitalarkivet (digitalarkivet.no) is the primary free resource for Norwegian church records with index and images; often more complete than FamilySearch for specific parishes.
Farm names (gaardnavne) indicate residence, not surname — 'Anders Monsen Bakke' and 'Anders Monsen' are the same person; farm name changes when family moves.
The -datter suffix was frequently abbreviated in records as d., dr., or dtr. — search for Halsteinsd. and variants.
Spelling was not standardized until 1917 — search name variants: Halstein/Hallstein/Halsten/Halstein, Unna/Una/Anne.
Duplicate registers exist from 1814 (intermittent to 1820, compulsory again 1870): priest's copy and sexton's copy were both sent to the regional state archive (Statsarkiv).
No civil registration in Norway until 1876 (statistical use only); for 1750-1900 the Lutheran church register is the sole vital registration system.
After 1830s, marriage records include fathers' names and birthplaces of both parties — a post-1830s marriage record is particularly informative.
Records are in Danish (pre-~1800) or Norwegian and commonly use Gothic handwriting; the FamilySearch Norwegian Genealogical Word List and Handwriting guide are essential aids.

localities.guide_markdown:
# Norway Locality Guide — Marriage Research (1750–1900)

## Jurisdictional Context
Norway (standardPlace: 'Norway', country-level since +872). For 1750–1900: under Danish crown until 1814, then personal union with Sweden 1814–1905. Standard printed register format introduced 1814. Counties renamed from *amt* to *fylke* in 1917. Jurisdiction: country → county → clerical district (prestegjeld) → parish (sogn). Parish is the key working unit.

## Naming Customs
Monsen (son of Mons) and Halsteinsdatter (daughter of Halstein) are classic patronymics. Patronymics changed each generation. Farm names indicate residence, not surname. Spelling unstandardized until 1917. Must know the parish to search effectively.

## Primary Record Type: Lutheran Church Records (Kirkebøker)
Marriage records contain: names, date, place of residence, bachelor/widow status, occupations, bondsmen (witnesses), banns dates. After 1830s: fathers' names and birthplaces. Couples married in bride's home parish. Duplicate sexton copies from 1814 (compulsory again 1870).

## Key Collections
- **Digitalarkivet** (free, index + images): https://www.digitalarkivet.no/en/
- **Norway, Church Books, 1797-1958** (FS collection 4237104): index + images — best FamilySearch option
- **Norway, Marriages, 1660-1926** (FS collection 1468080): index only, legacy/partial
- Ancestry ($): Norway Marriages 1600-1800 and 1660-1926
- MyHeritage ($): Norway Marriages 1660-1926 and Church Records 1815-1938
- Norwegian Historical Data Centre: https://www.rhd.uit.no/indexeng.html

## Civil Registration
No civil registration until 1876 (statistical only). Folkeregistre began 1915. Church records are sole vital registration system for 1750-1900.

## Supporting Records
Census (1801, 1865, 1870, 1875, 1891, 1900), farm books (bygdebøker), probate records (skifte), moving records (inn/out migration lists in church registers).
